Work on the handsome new hospital
building being erected as a part of the
insane asylum at Warm Springs is pro-
crossing rapidly. The walls are now
up to the first story.


The building is being erected by Drs.
Mitchell & Mussigbrod the insane asy-
lum contractors. 1t, with various other
Improvements now under course of con-
struction, will cost about S1O0 900.


While designed chiefly for hospital
purposes a portion Of the building may
be pressed into service for the perman-
ent occupancy of patients, for the num-
ber at the institution is growing. There
are now over 500 insane people at the
asylum, over 100 of whom have been
sent there since the first of the year.


Brick, stone and iron are the ma
terials to be used in the construction of
the new building. The foundation is of
granite. There is high basement and
above that two stories. The building
will be completed this fall.


The chief features of the new build
ing, aside from the many smaller rooms,
are two large wards and an operat ting
room. The latter, it is expected, will
be the finest of the kind in the West.
The idea in the construction of the hos
pital is to make it a model of its kind
equipped with every modern improve
ment. The walls are to be treated with
new preparation which allows abso-
lutely no lodgment for microbes. There
will be no corners in the rooms where
microbes could find a home, for all
functions of walls with floor and cell
ing will be rounded. Even the window
sashes and door easements will be
treated in the same way. The floors
are all to be tiled. The wards will be
commodious rooms, light and airy.


The several buildings comprising the
asylum are now crowded, and for the
proper care of the patients the contrac-
tors have found it necessary to erect
the new building


In addition to this structure, new
store rooms, work shops, lumber sheds,
stables and other necessary outbuild-
ings are being erected or reconstructed.


A visitor to the institution is struck
by the air of perfect cleanliness and
comfort that prevades the whole place.
Floors and walls are spotless, the at
mosphere of the buildings is pure and
wholesome, and the whole institution
seems to be managed on the most hy-
gienic basis.

During the session of 1897-'98 our Solons, who by this time had begun better to appreciate the wheel, amended the existing law as to rates of toll on railroads, and declared that bicycles should be deemed baggage and transported on the same terms as other baggage.

Later on, when the horseless carriage shows its mettle and proves itself a public benefactor, we may expect to hear of its receiving equal courtesies at the hands of the law, though as yet its movements are regarded with suspicion. Of course, we do not mean by the term "horseless carriage" a vehicle drawn by a mule. This latter combination, however valuable for practical purposes, will never command respect. The mule is the "filius nullus" of the equine race.

CITY OF MEXICO, Oct.—Miss Dorothy Bowman, a young woman of California, who is visiting Mexico, has arrived here from a climb to the very summit of Popocatepetl volcano. The fact that deep oil exists in Pleasants county can no longer be disputed. With the present outlook it may prove to be one of the richest Injun fields as well as being the most profitable and prolific Cow Run sand fields known.

Washington, May 7.—Captain H. L. Street, U. S. army, the commissary officer in charge of supplies sent to Cuba on the Coman since January 19, is in the city.

Captain Street has carried to Cuba 3,000,000 rations to be distributed to the Cubans since January 19. In excess of those rations he has taken to Cuba 100,000 cans of condensed milk, 500,000 cans of soups, consisting of oxtail, beef, chicken and some clam soup; also rice, sugar, coffee, pepper, soap, baking powder, fresh yeast. He has visited Havana, Sagua, Matanzas, Nuevitas, Cienfuegos, Trinidad and Tunis, turning his supplies over to the depot commissaries of those places.

"How do the Cubans receive these gifts?" Captain Street was asked.

"They take all they can get, and do not thank you a bit for it. That is the plain English of it," was his reply. "I think they are the most ungrateful selfish-set ever came across, and no one was stronger pro-Cuban than I was before the war was begun. Any other there will tell you the same thing."

"What do you regard as the present prospect of getting these people on a self-supporting basis?"

"If they desire to work I do not see why they could not be put on that basis now. A war has been over for some time. I was told by a gentleman who is running a big plantation near Nuevitas, a plantation carrying $2,000,000 in machinery, that he wanted to employ 2,000 men at $20 per month and rations. That is regarded as good pay for them. He could not get the men, and when I inquired why he could not get them he said: The government is feeding them and they do not have to work. The Vice-president of the railroad running out of Nuevitas told me he could give employment to 1,000 men if he could get them, but he could not. There are a mass of Cubans who were killed or died of disease during the war. They are largely in the interior, and it is necessary that they should have food. It is a question in my mind whether they get it. It is not possible to distribute relief supplies in Cuba as that work might be done in this country where there are organizations that could assist in the work. Our idea is that man will supply the women and children of his family before he supplies himself, but these Cubans supply themselves first, and it is a doubtful question what their families get."

The Phoenix Republican takes issue with the Los Angeles Times regarding the latter's statements concerning the eeding of the arid lands to the States and Territories, and the Times con demnation of Governor Murphy's (of Arizona) attitude on the question. The Republican protests that Governor Murphy has done more for Arizona than any other man in the Territory i; has made a-national reputation while in Congress, and is recognized as one ot the strongest men in the country. The Times rejoins that it has never intimated anything to the contrary, but that, forsooth, it does not follow as logical sequence that the views of Governor Murphy which favor the ced- ing of the lands to the States are wise or correct.

 The Republican says there is on present hope of getting Congress to vote money for the building of reser- voirs, because residents of the agri- cultural States east of the arid region are against further competition in the raising of crops, and that, therefore, we should all join in the movement for the cession of these lands to the States and Territories.

 This the Times maintains is a false premise. The idea that because the right road is a difficult one to travel. we should take to the broad and easy road that leads to destruction is pusillanimous, and unworthy of Amer jeans. The irrigation of the arid lands of the United States is a big question, involving the expenditure of a large amount of money. It always takes time to educate public opinion on these important questions and to get Congress to act.

 So it is with the great question of irrigating the arid lands, and so mak- ing homes for millions of American citizens, at no ultimate cost to the Government; but Congress is slowly but surely coming around to 8 reaIiza- tion of the great importance of this question, thanks, largely, to the inde- fatigable efforts of few public-spirit- ed citizens of the great West, backed by it's most influential newspapers. Every irrigation congress, and the recent congress at Wichita, has resolved in favor of national irrigation and against cession of the lands to the States and Territories. This has been done in spite of the strenuous efforts made by small number of interested persons to swing the conventions into an opposite channel. Should the efforts of these men prevail, which is not probable, Arizona would be one of the greatest sufferers, among the States and Territories, from such mistaken policy.

The Republican protests that Governor Murphy has done more for Arizona than any other man in the Territory; has made a national reputation while in Congress, and is recognized as one of the strongest men in the country. The Times rejoins that it has never intimated anything to the contrary, but that, forsooth, it does not follow as logical sequence that the views of Governor Murphy which favor the ceding of the lands to the States are wise or correct.

The Republican says there is no present hope of getting Congress to vote money for the building of reservoirs, because residents of the agricultural States east of the arid region are against further competition in the raising of crops, and that, therefore, we should all join in the movement for the cession of these lands to the States and Territories.

This the Times maintains is a false premise. The idea that because the right road is a difficult one to travel, we should take to the broad and easy road that leads to destruction is pusillanimous, and unworthy of Americans. The irrigation of the arid lands of the United States is a big question, involving the expenditure of a large amount of money. It always takes time to educate public opinion on these important questions and to get Congress to act.

So it is with the great question of irrigating the arid lands, and so making homes for millions of American citizens, at no ultimate cost to the Government; but Congress is slowly but surely coming around to realization of the great importance of this question, thanks, largely, to the indefatigable efforts of few public-spirited citizens of the great West, backed by its most influential newspapers. Every irrigation congress, and the recent congress at Wichita, has resolved in favor of national irrigation and against cession of the lands to the States and Territories. This has been done in spite of the strenuous efforts made by small number of interested persons to swing the conventions into an opposite channel. Should the efforts of these men prevail, which is not probable, Arizona would be one of the greatest sufferers, among the States and Territories, from such mistaken policy.

New York, Nov. 2.--The stock market took on a show of great animation and strength to-day. Some very striking net gains resulted from the day's trading. A close analysis shows, however, that the activity and strength were concentrated in comparatively few stocks. The general list, though higher in price at the closing to-day, developed little activity. The operations, which in the aggregate were large, amounted to a total of $4,000,000. Shares sold were largely confined to the professional element. The upward movement was obviously based upon the notably easier tone of the money market. The largest operations were by powerful pools and strong financial interests which have at command money resources outside the usual money market circles. The prevailing opinion in Wall street is that prices of stocks would move upward easily if the obstacle of stringent money were removed. The large outstanding short interest in stocks has been palpably easy for some time past and any indications of relaxation in the tightness of money makes them inclined to cover their short contracts. The professional pool operations in number of prominent stocks to-day were obviously directed against the bear contingent and with good success. It is very probable, however, that the large buying at other points is based on expectation of a rise in prices on account of a growing public interest in stocks. It is the period of the year when, under normal circumstances, the extra uses for money in the moving of the crops begins to show diminution, releasing large funds for employment in stock speculation. Outside the highly speculative industrials the movement in the railroads centered in the southwestern group. The special strength and activity in Southern Pacific helped the southwesterners and was based on current rumors of reimbursement of control. The belated movement in cotton was a factor of strength amongst both southern and southwestern railroads. There were special movements besides in Cleveland, Cin. and St. Louis and in Chesapeake and Ohio, and some demand for the coalers. The upward movement in the iron and steel stocks encountered difficulties as did that in Brooklyn Transit. Speculation in Leather continued on an enormous scale, the stock rising an extreme 1/4. The slaughter of the favorites continued at Tanforan Park yesterday, and for the time being the bookmaking fraternity appear to be masters of the situation. The races broke so nicely for the layers of odds that even the field books made money. For change, of six choices sent to the post, Aborigine, most shaky one, and Tullamore were the only ones to safely navigate the juicy going.

The menu contained no notable turf delicacies, the seven furlong handicap alone possessing any pretensions as to class. There were seven acceptances, and it was a most open betting affair. At post time Silver Tone, with 99 pounds up, had a slight call over Morinel, carrying Tommy Burns and 102 pounds. Spencer had the mount on Ostler Joe, the top-weight, and the black horse seemed well thought of, ruling third choice. When sent away King Carnival, a well touted one, hurried away in the lead, which he held for half the distance, followed by Ostler Joe and Morinel. Less than three furlongs from the stand Burns on the latter made an early move, quickly followed by Spencer with Joe. Weight told the last sixteenth and the black fellow under hard urging was storm's game mare. Silver Tone found all the wash-outs in the track and Johnson on Potente lost his bearings altogether at the stretch turn while taking deep water soundings.

A shabby bunch started in the half mile scramble for two-year-olds. After a zig zag journey Thorpe on Aborigine managed to down March Seven a length. St. Agnes, at one time favorite, was third.

Thorpe also piloted Pat Murphy over the mark winner of the five furlong dash following. Third choice in the ring, the roam horse under persuasive riding out gained on Toribio, the favorite, winning by a neck. Ricardo, well-played starter, took the show.

Forte, with Bullman in the saddle and favorite for the mile and furlong run, at no time seemed afflicted with speed, finishing third behind Jennie Reed and Coda. It was only a gallop for the first named mare which won all the way. Reolia was caught by the webbing at the start, never being prominent.

Billy Randall's patched up sprinter Tullamore captured the fourth event at six furlongs. Jack Martin rode him to perfection, and stalling off the challenge of Monda, beat that gelding out a neck, drawing away. Eddie Jones on Campus had to be content with third money.

Tommy Burns sat astride the winner of the afterpiece—Lothian. Montallade, a 10 to 1 outsider, nearly made a runaway race of it, leading to within forty yards of the wire, where Burns and his mount came up, downing the long shot a head. Spencer on the even money favorite Lodestar ran into the show.

I knew, however, that in an hour or so the moon would rise; and I thought that, without what particular reason I can not say; but it came into my head, and the good Lord put it there, perhaps.

Being by myself alone, the fancy came upon me that I was the only man left in the world. I could not hear a sound but the soft tapping of the waves as they rolled inshore, as they had rolled on this self-same spot thousands and thousands of years ago, and as they would roll for thousands and thousands more, till they rolled into eternity. We get thoughts now and again that we can not plumb, and can not take the measure of. If I were to set down the notions that came into my head as I walked up and down that solemn shore, you would hardly believe that I was not drawing on my imagination. I thought that the world was dead; that light was gone out of it for ever and ever; that it would be always night, world without end; and that sun, moon and stars would never shine again. I stopped and listened to the waves; and to my fevered fancy, they spoke language that I could understand; and as I stood still to listen to the unspoken words, which made me shudder, so awful were the suggestions they conveyed, that fear came upon me that if I did not move, and move quickly, I should be turned into stone, with ears to hear and eyes to see, but with all power of motion gone forever.

Then, as I forced myself to pace the shore, the waves again whispered to me, asking me to join them, and so put an end to everything; but I flung away the temptation and cried, "Never, never!" and was startled by the sound of my own voice, as if it were some strange monster that was speaking and not myself. And then came other fancies; shadows formed themselves into the semblance of places I was familiar with, into the shapes of men and women I had known. I saw them so plainly that at first I believed them to be real; there rose the little cottage at Brixton, with "Beecroft, Mariner" over the window, and my mother standing at the door looking down the street for me. That picture faded and melted into another: I and the child Mabel were together, I holding a shell to her ear, and she gazing in pleasant wonder into my shadowy face; then came that villain Bruce, and with him a dark mist of blood before my eyes, which blotted out the pictures and put an end to them. I shook myself roughly and turned aside to meet other fancies.

About a hundred yards to the left was high sand-rock, and as I turned toward it, I saw three old women, for all the world like witches, with pointed chins, and with crooked saplings in their hands. They were pointing with their long, bony fingers at something that lay at their feet. I had once seen three witches in a play, dancing round a cauldron, and these were like them. I waited for the fire to squirt up from the ground, and for themselves to commence to dance; but they stood quite still and motionless, bending toward each other so that their chins almost touched. I made a few steps forward—slowly and cautiously, for I did not know what kind of creatures might be living on these wild shores, and I dare to say being scared—and discovered that the three old witches were three bits of scrubby twigs sticking up out of the sand-rock.

Washington March 27.—Dr. A. Knapp, who was sent by the Department of Agriculture to Japan, China and the Philippines as an agricultural explorer, has returned to Washington and reported to Secretary Wilson the results of his labors.


He was instructed to investigate such products of the farms, fields and forests of those countries as might be of advantage to the agricultural industries of the United States. Some of the observations of Dr. Knapp relating to the products of Japan have already been published in a preliminary report on this branch of investigation; however, he has the following additional to say:


An fear of competition from Japan along agricultural lines may be dismissed. On the contrary, it must become a large consumer of farm products drawn from the United States. The diffusion of knowledge and the introduction of new industries in Japan have had the effect of more than doubling the cost of labor in the last ten years and, in proportion, of stimulating consumption by the common people.


Future progress must be mainly made in the direction of manufactures. In such event the food for the operatives, the cotton and other fibre material for the fabrics, the lumber and iron for the construction of the factories and much of the machinery will be drawn from the United States. Of the fabrics, cotton and wool alone have made much progress under the factory system, and this is owing to the fact that they were not produced to any extent in the empire, and hence no home system of manufacture had been established for them.


VALUE OF FOOD IMPORTS IN JAPAN.


The principal agricultural products imported by Japan are wheat, flour, sugar, cotton, butter, cheese and meat. The annual value of these articles is at present between $4,000,000 and $5,000,000 in gold. Under favorable treaty regulations Japan will import from the United States nearly all her flour, butter, cheese and meat, two-thirds of the raw cotton required, and from the Philippines rice.


Regarding China, the report says: The great area, the large per cent of fertile lands, and the enormous population of China, stagger the onset at the threshold of investigation. Here, however, in Japan radical changes in agricultural methods or products must be made slowly. If at all, because the food supply cannot be materially reduced or even changed with safety. Large areas devoted to fibre plants for the promotion of manufactures would be a dangerous invasion of the areas necessary for the food supply, and must be speedily followed by importations from the United States. Dr. Knapp is deeply impressed by the alert, industrious and frugal character of the Chinese.


AGRICULTURE IN THE PHILIPPINES.


From China Dr. Knapp proceeded to the Philippines. Arriving at Manila, he went by rail as far as San Fernando, passing through the rice section to the east and north of Manila, and on the sugar lands to the north. The yield to an acre, according to the best authorities, he found to be about one thousand pounds of milled rice on lands under rainfall irrigation solely and two thousand pounds on lands artificially irrigated, showing careless husbandry.


Dr. Knapp further says:


"The rich clay loam soil about San Fernando is well adapted to sugar-cane. In Luzon the methods of sugar farming are different from those practiced in the islands of Panay, Negros and Cebu. The sugar farms and factories are much more improved than in Luzon. Sugar lands produce from three thousand to eight thousand pounds an acre depending upon the soil. In Luzon the methods of sugar farming are different from those practiced in the islands of Panay, Negros and Cebu. The sugar is drained upon the open kettle plan. The proprietor furnishes land and supplies most of the hands for making the sugar and the molasses. The tenant, in theory, is allowed the..."

Philippine coffee, of which there were formerly many plantations, has a peculiarly rich and pleasant flavor. Cocoanuts, pineapples, oranges, bananas, grapes and many other fruits grow almost spontaneously.


The Philippine Islands abound in valuable wood for building furniture, dye woods and some yield very costly gums. According to the best authority, the islands pass to the United States with the title opened for settlement to soldiers, many of our young men will remain and become permanent settlers. Professor Charles T. Woods, Jr., A. B., who has been for two years Professor of French and German in the Woman's College and Richmond College, of this city, has resigned these positions to accept a professorship of Modern Languages at Swarthmore College near Philadelphia.

Mr. Woods begins his work in Swarthmore this month. The institution to which he goes is one of high standing, so the tender of a professorship in it is a compliment to him. He deserved it, having given entire satisfaction to the trustees of both Richmond and Woman's Colleges. Swarthmore has been fortunate in securing him.

The Woman's College and Richmond College have also been exceedingly fortunate in securing as Dr. Woods's successor Dr. T. J. Becker, A. B., Ph. D., of Baltimore. Prof. Becker, as was Dr. Woods, will be full Professor of Modern Languages in the Woman's College and assistant to President Boatwright in the professorship of those languages in Richmond College. He has just telegraphed his acceptance of both positions.

Dr. Becker is a native of Baltimore, was educated in the city schools there, and then graduated with both M. A. and the Ph. D. degrees from the Johns Hopkins University. He comes to Richmond highly recommended, and fine work may be expected of him.

ANOTHER NEW PROFESSOR.

The Woman's College makes another notable addition to its teaching force. Dr. James Nelson, president of this institution, has just been advised of Professor W. W. Lingle's acceptance of the Chair of Moral Philosophy.

Professor Lingle is an M. A. graduate of Davidson College, North Carolina. From Davidson Mr. Lingle went to Cornell University, where he spent two years under Professor Schooner, one of the most eminent teachers of Moral Philosophy in the country. The next two years he spent in pursuance of his studies at Leipzig. Professor Lingle is one of the best teachers of Moral Philosophy yet seen in Richmond. He is not unknown around people. He has been a recognized student in Union Theological Seminary of this city. His brother was also a professor in the seminary.

The remaining addition to the faculty of the college for the approaching session is Professor Jacob Reinhardt, of this city, to supplement the instruction in piano and violin.

The forty-sixth session of the Woman's College begins Thursday, the 21st of this month. Last year the attendance reached 155; this year the prospects are exceedingly bright.

For several years past Dr. Nelson has had associated with him as dean of the faculty Dr. Julian A. G. Chandler, an M. A. of William and Mary College, and Ph. D. of Johns Hopkins. Dr. Chandler, Professor of English and Pedagogy, in June, 1888, was elected to the Chair of History and English Literature in Richmond College. He has rendered exceedingly valuable services to both colleges and easily wins his way to the favor of the pupils under him and the student body at large. Dr. Chandler is the head of the Normal Department at the Woman's College, and for two years has had charge of a State summer normal.

THOMAS LECTURES POSTPONED.

Dr. James Thomas lectures of Richmond College will not take place this October, as was first planned. Prof. Benjamin W. Wheeler was engaged to deliver this series of lectures this year on "Old Greek Life." Since writing that he would come, Professor Wheeler has been elected president of the University of California, and has accepted. Now he has written Professor Winston, chairman of the Lecture Committee, that he would go to California the first of the fall and could not make the trip across the Continent so soon. He says that the lectures could be conveniently postponed until late winter or early spring when he would come. In the absence of Professor Winston, President Boatwright read the letter and agreed for the series to be delivered by Professor Wheeler later in the session.

PROFESSOR MITCHELL COMING.

Professor S. G. Mitchell, of the Chair of [Philosophy], but now pursuing course toward Ph. D. degree at the Chicago University, writes to President Boatwright that he will be here about September 18th. He will receive his degree before leaving this city. He writes that Professor Winston and his constant and hard work have been an inspiration to him, and are a source of comfort and joy.

The college will be open Thursday of this month. President Boatwright is much encouraged by it.

OPENING OF OTHER SCHOOLS.

The public schools of the city will begin September 4th, next Friday week. The first of opening will be devoted to returning former students, and Monday to enrolling new students.

All the public schools in Richmond will be about this time. The session of the College of Virginia opens September 28th, that of the University College of Medicine October 3rd. The Richmond Female Seminary opens Thursday, September 21st, and McCabe's and Motley's schools Monday, September 18th; McGuire's, September 20th. The smaller private schools open within a week of the same date or the other, and before the month ends the student body of Richmond and Manchester will reach the proportions of a great army.

of far-reaching importance in fix
ing the rights of minority stock
holders in their relations with

erty, the remedy sought in in

ant is not based on good law nor

amine the books and the records

junction.

combinations of corporations in
the shape of trusts for the pur-
pose of secretly carrying on and
exercising franchises granted by
State governments—and this in
defiance of prohibitory statutes—
it is of the utmost importance
that this right of stakeholder to
examine the workings and methods
of such combinations be given a
liberal construction. It, if not his
only, is the greatest safeguard
which the law provides against
mismanagement or treachery on
the part of those in control.

in this bill is the right of directors
to conceal from stockholders the
information as to the manner in
which they are using the prop
erty, the remedy sought in in
junction being to prevent him

obtain that information.

feared or threatened lawsuit.

ant is not based on good law nor
good equity. The injunction must
be dissolved."

The Harue appellee, is none other than Dr Narcissus Matas, a wealthy and skillful physician of Tucson. The story began in the province of Catalan, Spain, where the doctor was born and married. January 25.—The Republic, the official organ of the Philippines, announces that the congress at Malolos has adopted the Philippine constitution, passed a vote of confidence in Aguinaldo and empowered him to declare war on the Americans whenever he may deem it advisable.

General Superintendent, Charles A.
Tinker, of the Western Union Tele-
graph Company, has written for the
Telegraph Age a remarkably interest
ing paper, touching upon the eventful
period of the history of the United
States when the Civil War was rag
ing.


At that time Supt. Tinker, then a
mere boy, was in daily communication
with the president and saw him in all
his unparalleled simplicity. In telling
of the first time Supt. Tinker met "Old
Abe" in Pekin, Ill., before the great
emancipator became president, he
writes of the meeting:


"One afternoon, as I was sitting on
my high stool listening to the click of
the register, and waiting for Gus
toner, he came to the office, and look
ing over the tall railing, said: Mr. Op-
erator, I have always had curiosity
to see the telegraph work. You don't
seem to be very busy, and as I have
a half hour or so to wait for dinner,
wonder if you will not explain it to
me?" I replied, "Certainly, sir, I should
be pleased to do so," and inviting him
inside the gate I proceeded to show
him the working of the telegraph—ex-
plained the battery and its connection
to the instruments and the wires lead
ing thence out of the window and away
to the world without. I was encourage
d by the readiness with which he com-
prehended it all. He seemed to grasp
its intricacies, and remarked, "How
simple it is when you know it all!" I
called up Chicago, and requested the
operator to send a message to old Abe
Lincoln who was standing at my side.
He sent the usual complimentary greet
ing. Mr. Lincoln watched me closely
as I copied it from ear, and thought
that was the mystery of it all, as he
could not take it in. He wished me to
thank the Chicago operator, and say
that he was greatly pleased at the
opportunity to see the operation of the
telegraph. He then left me."


Some time after that young Tinker
entered the United States telegraph
service and most of the telegrams to
the president passed through his hands.
On the second nomination of Lincoln
he writes:


"During the progress of the Balti-
more convention by which Mr. Lin-
coln was nominated for second term,
one of his secretaries, Mr. Nicolay, who
attended the convention, kept the
president constantly advised of the pro-
ceedings. Finally came the message


quickly to the White House by an or-
derly. Shortly after the message had
gone, Mr. Lincoln came into the office,
and congratulated him upon his nom-
ination. He exclaimed: 'I hadn't heard
of it,' with some surprise. I explained
that I had sent Mr. Nicolay's message
over to the White House by an orderly.
He said: 'Well, I guess he took the
short cut. I came around by the public
highway!' I then showed him a copy
of the message. He read it half-haste,
and said: 'I guess you had better send
that over to the Madam. She will be as
much interested in it as me.'"


"It happened that when the message
announcing the nomination of Andrew
Johnson to the presidency was re-
ceived the president was in the office.
He read it carefully, and announced
aloud, 'When I thought possible he
might be the man. Perhaps he is
the best man, but...' rising
from his chair he passed out of the of-
fice leaving me impressed with the sig-
nificance of the unfinished doubt which,
in the light of subsequent events, be-
came a striking prophecy."


Supt. Tinker is also president of the
Lincoln-Elgin, and his tales of the dead
president are regarded as invaluable history that will
add much to the information to be handed
down to posterity."

hearts of the lone prospectors of the
outlying districts. Occupants of min-
ing cabins in the foothills now barri-
cade their doors when they lay down to
sleep at night, and a loaded shotgun
stands within reach. Moore's provisions
are believed to be almost exhausted,
and it is certain he will make an at-
tempt to replenish them at one of the
many cabins in the neighboring moun-
tains. If resistance is offered others
may fall victims to his unerring aim.
Every teamster who finds it necessary
to traverse the lonely mountain roads
carries a shotgun, and every prospector
who saunters into town from the foot-
hills is armed with a weapon of some
sort in anticipation of a meeting with
the desperate. Moore is the one man
in the county whom everybody fears.
He is as quick as a flash with rifle,
shotgun or revolver, can shoot with
marvellous accuracy and is of that
manner of man who would have little
hesitancy in shooting friend or foe
from behind if he thought they stood
between him and his freedom. Those
who know the outlaw believe that be-
fore he is captured some of his pur-
suers will fall.


In his dash for liberty Moore is ac-
companied by at least one faithful
friend, who has thus far proved a val-
uable ally to the fugitive in his flight
across the mountains. The authorities
declare Moore's trained dog is a potent
factor in his master's successful efforts
in eluding pursuit. The animal is in
deed a wonderful canine. Moore is
partially deaf and is compelled to carry
an ear trumpet, but his disadvantage
in this respect is fully made up by the
dog's wonderful instinct. The animal
is ever on the alert for approaching
footsteps or the sound of human voices.
The least murmur or the faintest foot-
fall attracts his attention and he warns
his master of the approaching danger
by a wag of his tail and a point to the
spot whence the sounds issue. He never
barks and should Moore happen to be
asleep the dog licks his face the mo-
ment he scents danger. These facts are
known to the authorities, as Moore has
in moments when he boasted that he
owned the smartest dog in the State
often displayed the brute's wonderful
qualities to admiring citizens. The
man hunters now searching the moun-
tains for the murderer are therefore al-
ways on the alert, because they know
Moore is informed of their presence
from afar.


There are many people here who be-
lieve Moore is hiding in some spot close
to his cabin on Little Deer Creek, near
the Charannet mine and scarcely any
body in the whole county believes the
fugitive has succeeded in getting any
distance out of the mountains. All the
roads and trails have been carefully
guarded since Saturday and there has
been little chance for him to escape.
The fact that the fugitive carried his
water bucket with him in his hurried
flight lends color to the general theory
of a rocky cavern or dry mining shaft close
to his cabin. Moore has often boasted
that he could hide himself within a
mile of the town where it would be
impossible for anybody to find him.


The killing of Kilroy undoubtedly
was premeditated and it is fair to pre-
sume that Moore expected to be placed
in position where he would be com-
plete to elude a horde of angry and
brave men anxious to bring him to ac-
count for his misdeeds. This theory is
borne out by the condition in which the
officers found Moore's cabin when they
arrived there shortly after the murder
was committed. Moore had been there
and removed everything that would be
useful to him in his flight. It was evident
the murderer had placed every-
thing in readiness for a hurried depart-
ure. On the floor was found a receipted
bill for $40 worth of groceries which
were supplied only three days before
by a local grocer. None of the pro-
visions was found in the cabin.

Coroner Hill held an inquest Yesterday
upon the body of Martin Shaughnessy
who died in St Marys Hospital on Octo-
Der 10 from the effect of injuries received
while at work in the planning mill of the
Excelsior Redwood Company. The testi-
mony showed that Shaughnessy, while
doing some work with the ripsaw, picked
up a piece of wood from the floor and
changed the belt from one pulley to an
other with it. The belt was running at
the time, and the stick was twisted in
such a way as to strike Shaughnessy in
the stomach


The jury returned a verdict that the de-
ceased met his death by an accident
caused by. gross carelessness of his en-
ployer. The apparatus for shifting the
belt was out of order and could not be
used, and Shaughnessy was obliged to use
the stick instead.

was hanged today for the murder of
John Linn.


Branton retired last night at

deputies. He walked upon the stage
unassisted and took his place on the
trap. When asked if he had anything
to say, he replied he had but little.


In a firm voice he told those present
that he did not want them to
hold any ill-will against his people on
account. He asked for sympathy and
prayers, and urged them to follow
God's way.


Sheriff Withers sprung the lever

mailed, and gave white tie to his
brother and left a Bible to his mother.

muscle. He assisted the Officers

execution, while a thousand or more
were in the street around the enclosure.

placed in a coffin and delivered to his
people.

paid the penalty of death was under
taking the life of John A. Linn, a
stockman of Condor, Gilliam County,

Her character was thoroughly singular. It was not unique, but never contradictory. You always knew in what direction to look for her, although sometimes your imagination might not stretch far enough, soar high enough, to overtake her. It may be worth while to bestow moments' consideration on the manner in which that character affected her relations and familiar society. People who plod straight along the beaten road footsteps of those uncommon travellers who go tramping over strange ground are in general traceable. You can distinguish the effects of their influence, whichever way it operates. If directly, it works with some, it founds its sort of school; their example and spirit continue to bear sway even after their existence is at end. With others, on the contrary, it works, and strongly, too, in an inverse ratio to what they would have wished. This was the case with Lady Mary, who preached us out of good breeding, regular economy, respect for authority, and many other commendable things, by dint of incessantly preaching us into them; and as her notions were ordinarily exaggerated rather than erroneous, one was at times half tempted to regret the certainty of their summary condemnation without appeal. Every act or opinion bordering on the great, the noble, the dignified, common workaday world had a chilling shadow of ridicule cast over it, as just suited to Lady Mary Coke. If you were caught supposing Lord Chatham and Lord Clarendon to have flourished together, concluding that James the First was Queen Elizabeth's eldest son, you had but to shrug your shoulders and cry, "Well, for my part, I don't pretend to Lady Mary Coke's amazing knowledge of history, and you came off with flying colors." There might sometimes be malice in the matter in its own mischievous contention as to who should scandalize Lady Mary most. Her silly genealogy and etiquette made one flippant girl think it pretty air not to know how she was related to her first cousin; and another assert she could not see the use of bowing and curtsying. The treatise became more bearish after one of Lady Mary's lectures, resuming tolerable good manners as the taste of it wore off. To wind up all with something like a moral, be it remembered that we do the worst office possible to whatever is serious or praiseworthy by carrying it to an extreme which must inevitably excite laughter; but at the same time be it confessed that we cannot habituate ourselves to look constantly and exclusively at the ridiculous side of almost any object, without in some degree injuring, if not debasing, our own minds.

Still another passage, which occurs in a letter to Mrs. Lockhart, is rather a shrewd comment on a phase of human nature which is quite as much in evidence now as in Lady Louisa's time.

Why do very young people who do not yet know the existing world, so far partake of the spirit of their age as to judge according to it, or to their parents and foretathers when they first out? What suggested it to me in my own day all mothers strictly forbade their daughters to read Rousseau's "Nouvelle Heloise," and all daughters, of course, longed to read nothing so much. I knew one young lady who owned to me that she stole reading of it standing on the top steps of her father's library ladder; and another who procured it and carried it into the country with her on her wedding day, in first fruits of being her own mistress. To say in truth, I believe no book ever did so much mischief. Yet within these few years I happened to hear a girl of very warm feeling, enthusiastic, romantic, just the person whose head it would have turned of old, declare she had tried to read it, but been so disgusted that she threw it away, before she got through half the first volume.

Many parents of today have pondered over this problem. Why should the children of those who delighted in "The Wide Wide World" and the "Rollo Books"—as thousands of children did in the last generation—refuse these works as prosy and silly? Why should Thackeray and Dickens lie on the upper shelves of many?

"Thatcher" exclaimed my client, "have you been for holiday?" "No," I replied. "But you look" he continued "as if you had just come from the seaside." Taking the week throughout, and with a good walk on Sundays, I get perhaps as much fresh air as men who lead outdoor lives.

Then, as to physical exercise, I have ample resources in my home. The Council Committees Have

Their Business Prepared for This

Afternoons Meeting—Globe Valve

Closet and Paving Ordinances to

Go Through—Closet Ordinance Was

Held Up Pending the Location Of

This Class of Closets.

The indications are that the City Coun-

cil will not have voluminous lot of busi-

ness to dispose of this afternoon. Several

paving ordinances are to be introduced,

and the globe valve closet ordinance

which has been hanging fire for some

time, will also be put on its passage.

There is not understood to be any objec-

tion to the passage of these measures.

This is the time when Council experien-

ces its dullest season. The routine busi-

ness is being transacted without any ex-

tra effort to introduce radical measures.

During last week all the committees were

busy with matters which had been re-

ferred to them for to-day's meeting. At

the last meeting were submitted a larger

number of petitions and other communica-

tions. While the committees have

been kept busy getting these matters

off their hands, it is understood most of

the business has been prepared for Coun-

cil.

The finance committee met yesterday af-

ternoon. Among the matters referred to

it was the petition of hackmen asking

that they be allowed to use double team

badge for one-horse vehicles. Their rea-

son for the request is that they found it

necessary to attach double teams to their

hacks when the soldiers were in Savan-

nah, but since their departure, and the

consequent lessening of traffic, only one

horse has been attached to the same ve-

hicles. Under the city ordinance hack

men must have badges for the vehicles

they run. When the violation was discov-

ered the police nabbed them, and they

have now appealed for an exemption in

their case. The committee recognizes that

exceptions of this kind are not good pre-

cedents, but it is stated the petition will

likely be reported upon favorably. The

city is forced to either grant the petition

or compel the hackmen to use double

teams, as their badges call for. The most

important matter to settle was whether

the men came by the badges honestly, or

whether there had been trading which de-

creased the city's revenue. The commit-

tee was satisfied everything was straight.

at some length was issuing licenses to

petitioner desired to attract crowds by

musical entertainment. The license is $50

ory law, and the object of the petitioner,

done is not known, but there are members

of the committee who object to the use of

the streets for this purpose.

payers in Savannah who have vacant

rooms and vacant lots for rent," said Al-

derman Thomas, "I am not inclined to fa-

The Cleveland Iron Trade Review Resume

Summary of the Week in Iron Circles.

With the opening of navigation for 1900 six months oil, the bulk of the ore that is to be shipped next season is covered by charters or provided for in bouts owned by producers. In the past week further business was done at $120 from the head of the lake, $110 and $120 from Marquette and $110 from Escanaba. The Rockefeller interest is now credited with vessel capacity, either of its own or chartered, considerably in excess of 100,000 tons. Reports to the contrary notwithstanding, it seems settled that it will not have more than 900,000 tons of Carnegie-Oliver ore to haul, this coming from the Mountain Iron mine. Add to this 10,000 tons under contract, and the probable output of the Lake Superior Consolidated iron mines, and there is still left a tonnage of between 500,000 and 600,000, a portion of which is no doubt to be applied on the ore of a connected ore selling firm. The Carnegie Oliver order for new vessels was increased from five to six with an option on a seventh, thus taking up well into next year all the berths of the American Shipbuilding Co., on which vessels of modern size can be accommodated. There has been purchased for the Carnegie fleet, in addition to the Clarence A. Black mentioned last week, the steamer Linn and the barge Darlington. Other vessels are under option and further purchases may be announced later. It is stated that with the 900,000 tons the Rockefeller fleet will haul for it, the Carnegie interest has now quite fully provided for its tonnage needs for next year, or will have done so when pending deals are closed. The main contingency is to the portion of next season for which the boats to be built will be available. As indicated last week, the passing of vessel property into the hands of ore producers has been going on very rapidly. The vessel company unidentified with the American Steel & Wire Co. bought in the past week the two vessels recently ordered by A. Y. Wolvin. They will go into the Marquette, Cleve, trade, carrying something over 5,000 tons each. The same company bought also the steamer W. H. Gilbert. Its fleet is now capable of carrying over 1,000,000 tons of ore per year, or considerably more than the present capacity of American Mining Co. mines.

It is now expected that meeting of ore men will be held in the next five weeks, and the closing of ore business will doubtless follow soon. Some diversity of view appears as to the price that should be asked. There are conservatives and there are those who favor larger advance than has been seriously discussed thus far. It does not appear that any sales have been made beyond those recently reported, in which high phosphorus ores of the Crystal Falls district were quite fully sold at $1 a ton. These ores run from 50 to 60 per cent in iron and from 0.4 to 0.9 per cent in phosphorus.

back in his pocket and someone step
ped along and picked it UP. Anyway

The weather for the past three months
has been pleasant surprise to the people
who have spent their first winter here,
writes Consul J. C. McCook from Dawson,
under date of February 8. The coolest
weather we have had was between the
8th and 18th of November, the thermome-
ter registering 20 to 30 degrees below zero.
The month of December was ideal winter
weather, the thermometer then only reg-
istering around zero, and there being no
wind, so to speak, the air was as pleasant
as in November weather in the Middle
states. In January we had a couple of
weeks of very cold weather, but nothing
to be dreaded when one is warmly clad,
with the extremities of the body well pro-
tected against frost bites. While there
have been a great many cases of frozen
limbs, and amputation is sometimes nee-
ssary, such cases mostly came from long
continued exposure on particularly cold
days, or from exhaustion, or getting the
feet wet on stampedes.

Stampeding to relocate claims where
owners failed to do the necessary repre-
sentation work, or to some reported to-
morrow said to be good, has been very fre-
quent all winter. The majority of such
stampedes, however, proved failures; for
instance, in the first week of January
a stampede took place from Dawson down
the Yukon river on which some 80 men,

whom were some well-known, rich mine
owners, who would not be expected to go
out stampeding unless they had some in-
formation of positive character, any
one who could get a dog or two and a
sled and some provisions together started.
After travelling all night, a coup of war
was held by those who were in the secret
of the coveted locality. Heads were
counted, and, finding there were more in
camp than there could possibly be claims
at stake, the leaders concluded not to go
farther, but to starve out those who had
brought only a few days' provisions along.

Many came back to Dawson for more
provisions and started in again in the
effort to regain their former position.
Finally, the leaders made an onward
movement up creeks across divides and
hills, now having to make new trails in
the snow, unfortunately lost the proper
direction to the supposed goal. They had,
therefore, made retreat to Dawson,
returning exhausted and weary, and many
with frosted limbs after a week of fruit-
less search. There have been, however,
some successful relocations of good claims
this winter, which will pay the possessors
handsomely for all the trouble and hard
ships they have undergone.

The winter here as a whole, in my judg-
ment, is preferable to summer, as travel
over creeks and trails is much easier
and is not subject to the occurrence for one
to travel sixty miles in a
single day with a couple of dogs starting
at dawn and completing the trip.

Mr. John SHELTON Williams president of the Georgia and Alabama Railroad and the head of the big syndicate that recently bought a controlling share in the stock of the Seaboard Air Line, was in the city yesterday.

Mr. Williams was seen by a representative of the Morning News. He was very busy. He left last night for his home at Richmond.

The new power in the Seaboard's affairs, however found time to say that the big cut that has been made by that road in cotton rates from Atlanta and Athens to Portsmouth, is not a consequence of the deal through which he and his associates secured control of the road. Mr. Williams would not intimate, though, whether he was in accord with the cut or whether the policy of getting business, even though rates had to suffer, was that which will be followed by the Air Line.

Mr. Williams said the transfer to the syndicate has been made, but that nothing in the way of organization or reorganization has yet been effected. He did not say when the shake up, if shake up there is to be, among the officials of the big system will come.

The cut made by the Seaboard to Portsmouth, or to Norfolk, as the cities lie virtually together, was one of 2 cents on the hundred, thus bringing it down to 1/2 cents. The Central Railroad, the principal route from these cities to Savannah, will meet the cut at once, thus bringing its rate to 10 cents on the hundred, as there is a differential in the rates in favor of Savannah in Atlanta and Athens territory.

An effort was made yesterday to obtain the Central Railroad's side of the question, but none of its freight officials were in the city. President Conner and Vice President Egan were also absent. It simply became a necessity for the Central to make the reduction to meet the Seaboard's slash, however, as the road would get no cotton from the cities from which the rates are cut if shippers could send to Norfolk for 1/2 cents hundred pounds less than to Savannah.

Cotton men do not see that the cut is to have any special effect on Norfolk's, Savannah's or any of the ports' receipts to which the reduction is to be met by other lines. As the rates will remain relatively the same, there will be no difference in the situation. The same differential will have the tendency to give Savannah the share of freight that should come from its legitimate territory, and it is believed the receipts at the several ports will not be materially affected.

The reduced rates went into effect yesterday. It is believed as soon as the roads have all put their rates on the reduced equality notice will be given to the Commerce commission and the state commission of an intention to advance to the old figures. This advance cannot be made, however, until ten days after notice of the intention is given, so that, as a great deal of cotton may be expected to move during the season of low rates, the railroads will lose considerable, and the owners of cotton will be the gainers.

The Seaboard made the cut because it thought the other roads interested in handling cotton from the points from which the cut was made had not been "acting fair." RENNES FRANCE. August 8.—Following are the proceedings in detail of the Dreyfus court-martial to-day:

The temperance on the stage of the properties of M. Bertillon, the distinguished anthropometrist, was the signal for an outburst of hilarity on the part of the audience. The scenes of yesterday were repeated. The prisoner was apparently quite indifferent to what was going on, and the judges and counsel alone attempted to follow the specialist in his interminable cryptographic problems.

As the comedy was prolonged, it grew wearisome that the audience brought out newspapers and chatted in low tones. M. Bertillon, at one point, advanced alleged fresh proofs against the prisoner, namely, in the Dreyfus papers seized at the War Office, and in which, the specialist said, he found that two words had been traced. As he proceeded, the witness became imbedded in paraphernalia. His words, delivered in funereal tones, began to fail upon the judges, who finally only paid the most cursory attention to the examples he submitted.

DREYFUS DISDAINFUL.

One of M. Bertillon's demonstrations was handed to Dreyfus, who closely scrutinized it, and returned the paper with a disdainful shrug of his shoulders and without uttering a word.

In summing up the results of his test, M. Bertillon said:

"Fully understanding the responsibility of so positive statement, on my soul and conscience I declare to-day, as I did in 1894 on my oath, that the bordereau is the work of the prisoner here." (Sensation)

Dreyfus heard this assertion unmoved.

HYPOTHESIS AS TO ESTERHAZY.

The witness was asked by the court how he explained the similarity of the handwriting of the bordereau and that of Esterhazy, to which he replied that since 1894 Esterhazy may have practiced imitating writing of the bordereau in order to render possible the substitution of himself for the prisoner. In support of this theory, M. Bertillon produced a fresh array of plates which, he alleged, proved his hypothesis in regard to Esterhazy.

"Esterhazy," exclaimed M. Bertillon, "is a man of straw, and a scoundrel."

There was a sensation in court at this remark, which was turned to laughter as the witness, in his excitement, knocked his portfolios to the ground.

M. Demange asked M. Bertillon if he had submitted Esterhazy's handwriting to the same tests as the bordereau.

The witness replied in the affirmative, explaining, however, that the tests were less complete than in the case of the prisoner.

Counsel reminded the witness that he said in 1894 that he found in the bordereau a photographic signature—"A. Alfred Dreyfus."

M. Bertillon replied that he was not now positive on this point, to which, he added, he attached no importance whatever.

BERTILLON CONFUSED.

Referring to M. Bertillon's statement yesterday that he found in the bordereau words Dreyfus was in the habit of using in documents of the War Office, M. Demange asked how the witness accounted for this, and the specialist explained with some confusion, that it was "a necessary counterpart of the precautions taken by the prisoner when he wrote the bordereau, in order to make out that he was the victim of a plot" (Sensation).

M. Labor asked M. Bertillon how he reconciled the result of the present experiments—namely, that the bordereau was written by Dreyfus, tracing Esterhazy's handwriting with his opinion in 1894, that the bordereau was written by Dreyfus, unless it had been most carefully forged.

INJUSTICE TO PRISONER.

To this M. Bertillon replied that it was remarked that the forgery was then of such a nature as to constitute proof in favor of Dreyfus, yet to-day it is made proof against him.

Continuing, counsel said: "Since the witness admits that Esterhazy has written by the same mathematical methods as Dreyfus, why has he attributed the bordereau to Dreyfus rather than to Esterhazy?"

M. Bertillon: "It was on Dreyfus's blotting-pad that the keyword, 'interest,' was found, and Esterhazy might have had access to this word."

M. Labor: "Does M. Bertillon admit that Esterhazy is a traitor?"

Colonel Jouaust refused to put the question to the witness. (Sensation)

M. Labor, continuing his questions, asked M. Bertillon's opinion as to what system of defence might have been employed by the writer of the bordereau, if the document had been found by him.

The witness, in confused and almost inaudible tone, declared the prisoner would then have maintained that the document was forgery, and would have adduced it as proof of a plot.

Replying to further questions, M. Bertillon admitted he had discovered in Esterhazy's writing peculiarities similar to those in the bordereau.

DREYFUS EXPLAINS HIS "OH, THE WRETCH"

After a short incidental discussion of the Weyl forgery, which, it was believed, was perpetrated by order of the Prefect of Police, Colonel Jouaust asked the prisoner if he had anything to say in reply to the witness, and the attention of all present was immediately riveted on Dreyfus. Dreyfus explained how the exclamation, "Oh, the wretch!" escaped his lips.

"M. Bertillon," the prisoner said, "was constantly turning to me while testifying and calling me the guilty man. I retorted 'Wretch' to him. These are the circumstances under which I uttered the word.

"I have nothing to reply to the deposition of the witness, but there is one thing of which I am absolutely sure, and that is that I am not the writer of the bordereau."

world, nor is it strange that the people
of Europe look to New York with ever
increasing amazement.

strated in many ways. 1t is democratic

Principal Mather, of the Boardman school, says that in September there is prospect of new class of at least two hundred and fifty members entering the school. This will make a membership at the school of about four hundred and fifty. On that basis he estimates that the cost per capita will be about sixty dollars. Last year the cost was about ninety-five dollars. At Hillhouse the estimated cost per capita for next year is about fifty dollars. Principal Mather says that when the school is filled up the cost per capita will be no more than in any other high school.

A descendant of General Israel Putnam died at her home in Worcester, Mass., Saturday afternoon from injuries received by fall from an electric car January 31, and kidney trouble which developed. Mrs. Wall was born in Pomfret in 1828, and was married in Daniel Sprout. They lived in Southbridge, and twenty years ago moved to Worcester. She was of charitable disposition and did much good in an unassuming way. She was member of Plymouth church, of the auxiliary board of the Y. M. C. A., and connected with the Y. W. C. A. Her husband and two children, James H. and Sarah L. Wall, both of Worcester, survive. She also leaves two brothers, William Newell of Summit, R. I., and Daniel Newell of Providence. Mrs. Wall was the daughter of William and Lucy Wall, and on her father's side was a descendant of General Israel Putnam.

structure. We must lay stone on stone
around the rising framework to fashion
the image of the mind. So must we pile
thought on thought, cement resolution
to resolution till anon the Will's firm at-
titude is fixed, and our characters ap-
proach completion.

By what manner of thought shall such
force, mere resistance sufficient? I think
not. Resistance and non-recognition are
the two key notes. Merely to resist a
wrong is not in itself sufficient to trans-
form characteristic. If you gaze, how-

may hypnotize you by his superior charms.
But cry to Satan: Get thee behind me—

snake. To relieve the imagination, turn
on the light; if you would see different
pictures than you are wont to behold,

are looking for roses, do not linger in
stubble-fields. If you wish to behold an
Apollo, do not gaze at Callahan. Look
at what you wish to see. If you want
virtue do not gaze on vice. If you prefer

can gaze so long at the dark spots in the

Miss SADIE O'CHAIN, My dear,
your letter which I received a few days ago will tell you something of my condition and the time I have had since landing in Manila. We broke camp near Cauayan and left with Gen. Lawton's brigade the 22nd April for the interior of this hot island. We shortly fought with the insurgents. We cut off all communication with the outside world and marched towards the mountains with the enemy on all sides. We had several small battles in a few days, killing many of the enemy and losing many of our own, either killed or wounded. We all have to read of it in the papers when we have had a fight resulting in the defeat of the enemy. We fought three miles further and had another fight with the same results. We have had a great many battles but will not recount them now.

I know enough that getting used to being shot is not any better than did many others. We stood in places where the bullets were raining thick, making it impossible for one to escape, but I have not been hit yet. No telling when I may be killed, but I have an abiding faith in my Maker who watches over the desolation and hopes I am getting along alive.

I take care to protect myself when possible, but when I have exposed my company to the providence of the enemy, I have not been that lucky. A fellow broke out and gave us the alarm, and the company would have been all slaughtered without it. We brought the brave fellows with us with the loss only being small.

Don't credit us for what we do here. The regulars do the fighting and the volunteers get the credit. They mix with the 2nd and Bird artillery, and the volunteers are the only ones who get praise. They have their correspondents right along with them, and they always have time to write glowing reports of their deeds. The regulars have correspondents that have no time to write, but only to fight and think of duty, and that settles it.

The people in the town don't make a statement about matters here. We have a poor opinion of these negroes here. We fed them and they were fighting the next day. They are strange people. They have rather changes of clothes apiece which they carry with them. They say they are friends and would carry our flag, and five minutes later be shooting from a bamboo thicket to our advantage, knowing they do so from every bamboo thicket. They would murder anyone they chance, and run around the day and beg like a dog for something to eat. They don't want to fight here, but they follow the rough rule. They are a band of murderers, thieves, and cutthroats. They murder their own people and don't fight for freedom, but long to divide the goods while their officers divide them. Don't talk to me about these people; they are free, but they would be murderers another week. They surrender today, and tomorrow there are still many of them who would be soldiers.

They fight for what they can get out of it. The people who read papers which condemn this inhuman fighting since we have been here would come here and after a while they would think differently. We have been quartered here in houses and for two months received the BRECKE News, which had letters in its column like home again. Write often. We don't know how to write, do don't know how to do. I will write you again in a few months. Farewell for this time.

Lovingly,

GEORGE W. O'CHAIN,
Sergeant Co. M 3rd Infantry Manila, P. I.

tween gendarmes and disappointed
Cuban soldiers at Cuevitas, where the
payment of the Cuban troops is pro-
ceedings. The imperfect lists have
caused great dissatisfaction and the

preserve order among the applicants
and protect Col. Moale, the officer hav-
ing charge of the money. Suddenly
Capt. Baliat, who was mounted, was
surrounded by a mob, struck by stones

men promptly fired vOlley into the
mob. Three persons were instantly
killed and Is wounded, two of whom
died Wednesday morning. Col.

money office, but took no part in the
fighting. For a few minutes there was
a lively conflict, carbines and machetes

colored Cuban soldiers. Payment has

Editor Camera: A despatch in your
paper of Monday evening last, to the ef-
fect that the appropriation of 1896 for
the construction of the Buchanan pass
wagon road had lapsed, came as a thun-
derbolt in clear sky. After some con-
sideration of the subject, I am inclined
to think there is a mistake somewhere
and that the appropriation is still avail-
able. Let us see what the status is.


The bill of 1895, after stating the
amount appropriated for the road, $50,000,
describing the route, and naming
the officials who should superintend its
construction, sets out the following con-
dition: That if on making a
survey and estimate of the cost of said
wagon road, it is found that the amount
herein appropriated is not sufficient to
complete the said wagon road, then no
part of the appropriation herein provided
for it shall be used, except so much there
of as shall be necessary to make such
survey, unless the board of county com-
missioners or other responsible parties
of said Grand and Boulder counties shall
agree to furnish the amount required in
excess of this appropriation, and shall
furnish to said commissioners satisfac-
tory proof thereof upon request, and
forthcoming on demand of such commit-
sioners or the contractor, on the compile-
tion of such wagon road.


Soon after the passage of the bill a
survey and estimate was made and the
cost found to be about thirty thousand
dollars. The appropriation was of course
insufficient and the road could not be
constructed until the counties or private
individuals should make up the deficien-
cy. But there is in the bill no limit as
to time in which the deficiency may be
made up. That bill is law and has not
been amended nor repealed. It must
still stand unless some other statutory
provision or rule of law declares, after a
certain time, forfeiture. But no such
statute or rule seems to exist. Further-
more there ought to be some judicial as-
certainment of the failure of the counties
and citizens to act upon the proposition
that if they made good the deficiency,
the road would be built. But so far as
is known, no such judicial action has
been taken. The auditor in relation to
this matter, is a mere ministerial officer
and could not judicially inquire into it.
The legislature doubtless could take
such action, but instead of so doing, it
has done quite the reverse, for in its ap-
propriation this year it employs
these words: That in addition to the
amount appropriated by act approved
April 1895, for the construction of the
road herein described, there is hereby
the further sum of seven
thousand five hundred dollars, etc.

all doubt of its view as to the continue-

available for the construction of the

tee can do no harm and may be able to

Do Men Really believe in Immortality?
To THE EDITOR OF THE SUN—Sir: I read
to-day an anecdote in a religious paper which
raises the question in my mind: do people really
believe in an Immortality of perfect happiness
in a future state? It is the story of a little girl
at a summer hotel, who exclaimed how nice it was
when she was told that her little playmate had
gone to live in Heaven with Jesus, where she
would meet her little sister and two of her
brothers, who had gone before.

That was an instance of unquestioning belief,
and like belief in all Christians would make
death a joyful translation both for themselves
and for those they love. If we are confident of
making infinite gain by dying, have no doubt
on the subject. Why should we not be so kind to
die, and how selfish is it for us to lament the
cause those we love have won the prize by pass-
ing into the better life little before ourselves?

If men really believed in immortality as
Christianity teaches it, wouldn't the whole
course of human conduct be changed? Why
should they toil and strive for the immoral prize,
when their only satisfactory and ever
lasting life is not to begin until after
death? Why should they expend their energy
in keeping up wealth for themselves and their
children and chasing earthly glories when they
believe with faith which passes knowledge
that all this strife is silly vanity, compared
with the real fullness of joy and oppor-
tunity in a life beyond the grave? Or what
consequence is anything that happens in this
mortal life by the side of an everlasting life to come?

If people believed as this little girl believes,
in the actuality of future and immortal exis-
tence and perfect happiness, what else would
they do? What other thought would be in their
minds except running the conditions necessary
to get title to the mansions in the skies?

The argument is constantly used that men
naturally and unthinkingly believe in immortality. It seems to me on the contrary that
their whole procedure in this life indicates that
such faith is, or that it is but a dim
and doubtful hope. Preachers of Christianity
more especially at this time, are laying stress
on ameliorating earthly lives, worthless as they
are, as a preparation for the life to come,
if they believe honestly the Christian doc-
trine of immortality taught by them.

Do men really believe in this dogma of immortality? As it seems to me, no.

Interest was also rather poorly distributed, as few stocks furnished a disproportionate part of the total trading. These were notably Southern Pacific, United States Leather shares, and Brooklyn Rapid Transit. The day's news was meagre and without particular significance. The London market showed general declines, probably because of the unsatisfactory state of things in South Africa, and foreign houses were sellers of stocks in this market to limited extent.

and 1000 warriors who seemed les

Even though we constantly hear it, the position of 1900 will communicate the birth of the new century on New Year's Eve, although we commemorate it in the new century. The year 1900 is the very last evening before the new century. The dawn will not begin until the midnight, and it is thus:

This seemingly difficult problem is really very easy of solution, a matter of twelve units. The number 12 is a part of the dozen. There was no 0, the tenth year was 1 and the hundredth year of a century was the year 100.

Lizzie Cassidy, the 19-months-old daughter OF Thomas Cassidy, laborer, OF 100 York street, Brooklyn, disappeared from her home on July 2, having apparently been stolen. She was restored to her parents yesterday afternoon in good condition. There was something so queer about the discovery of the child that the police who had practically dropped the case, will now resume their investigations. They think that possibly if they can find out who was responsible for the return of the baby they will be able to guess who stole it.

Mrs. Annie Gray of 50 Willoughby street, Brooklyn, is Thomas Cassidy's sister.

"A well-dressed woman came to my house at noon to-day," Mrs. Gray said last night, "and told me where little Lizzie was. The woman said that she had been to the Gerry society rooms in Manhattan looking for some babies and saw ours. She knew it was ours, she said, because it tallied with all the descriptions which she had read. Then from the Gerry rooms she came over to Brooklyn, but didn't think then to go and tell Mrs. Cassidy. Instead she went to call on some friends on Willoughby street who happened to live near me. There she happened to mention what she had found, and the friends told her that the child's aunt lived nearby. That was myself. She came right over here and told me all about it. She didn't tell me her name and address, and wouldn't say who the Willoughby street neighbors were who had told her about me. The woman was well dressed and about 40 years old. I didn't stop then to ask her much about herself but hurried right over to New York to get the baby. I didn't tell Mrs. Cassidy, for fear of disappointing her with another false report. But it wasn't false. It was our baby sure enough, and I claimed it. The Gerry people wouldn't let me have it, but said that it must be identified by the mother. Then I hurried home to get my sister-in-law. We must have passed each other; I found that another person had been to give her the same information, and that she had gone to New York."

Mrs. Cassidy said to the reporter:

"About noon a short, stout man with reddish mustache came to my house and told me that my baby was in his society's rooms over in New York and that I had better hurry over and get it, as it was going to be put in a home. I hurried over to the Gerry society, and there they got it. They told me that the baby was found about twelve days ago at Ninth avenue high stoop, with a little boy about 4 years old.

The boy told the policeman who found them that Lizzie was his sister and that they had both been sent away from home. The little boy lied. The policeman took them both to the Gerry society, where they were put down on the books as unknown children.

We have no idea where the baby was during the first twelve days that it was away from us. Wherever she was she was well cared for. When she disappeared she wore black shoes. On Ninth avenue she had on a new pair of tan shoes. Her clothing was all different, too, and of good quality. She was in good physical condition."

At the Cassidy home in York street last night there was mingled rejoicing and indignation. The neighbors and relatives who went there with kegs of beer at their own expense shared the parents of the child the indignation.

There is a scar on its right shoulder; another on its forehead. It was in the newspapers and sent to the Gerry society and the police when the child was first lost.
